strengths: Clean, well-motivated theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 rigorously shows that combining a bounded proper scoring rule (Brier) with correctness reward jointly incentivizes calibration and accuracy, and the paper carefully explains why unbounded rules like log-loss fail this property (with a nice toy bandit experiment in Appendix E demonstrating the reward-hacking failure mode concretely).

Extensive and convincing empirical evaluation: results span in-domain and 6-7 out-of-domain datasets across both factual QA (HotpotQA) and math reasoning, with multiple strong baselines (BCE/Brier classifiers, linear probes, answer-probability, abstention-RL, other calibration-RL variants) and bootstrap confidence intervals.

Strong ablation studies isolating the contribution of explicit uncertainty analysis vs. the calibration-aware reward (Section 4.6, Table 2), providing clear mechanistic insight into what drives the improvements.
Generalization checks across model families (Qwen2.5, Qwen3, OLMo-2) in Appendix F strengthen confidence that findings are not specific to one base model.

Useful downstream demonstrations that verbalized confidence improves test-time scaling (confidence-weighted majority vote, best-of-N) and that RLCR improves self-consistency of confidence across reasoning chains, extending the practical relevance beyond calibration metrics alone.

High transparency and reproducibility effort: detailed training/eval setups, prompts, and honest discussion of limitations (e.g., SFT+RLCR OOD accuracy drop investigated and partially explained in Appendix J, comparison to closely related concurrent RL-calibration works clearly delineated in Related Work).
weaknesses: Absolute out-of-domain calibration error remains high even for RLCR (e.g., ECE 0.21 on OOD averaged for HotpotQA-trained models), and the paper's own inter-solution consistency analysis (Fig. 4b) shows persistent overconfidence OOD, tempering the practical significance of the gains.

The theoretical result (Theorem 1) is a relatively straightforward application of proper scoring rule theory to a two-term reward; the core novelty is more empirical/engineering (structured CoT + Brier reward) than deeply theoretical, and the framing as a proof-heavy contribution may overstate its technical novelty relative to closely related concurrent work (Xu et al. 2024; Stangel et al. 2025) which the paper itself acknowledges as most closely related.

Accuracy gains from RLCR over RLVR are inconsistent and sometimes RLCR is a few points worse in accuracy (e.g., HotpotQA in-domain 62.1% vs 63.0%), so the 'no cost in accuracy' claim is only approximately true empirically, not always exactly matching the RLVR baseline.

Evaluation relies partly on LLM-as-a-judge (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) for several OOD datasets (TriviaQA, SimpleQA, CommonsenseQA, GPQA), which introduces potential noise/bias into both accuracy and calibration metrics that is not deeply analyzed.

The SFT+RLCR variant's OOD accuracy collapse (43.8%) and its partial fix via a one-line prompt tweak (Appendix J) raises concerns about the robustness/reproducibility of reported numbers and suggests results can be sensitive to prompt engineering in ways not fully controlled for across all reported baselines.

Training and evaluation datasets are somewhat narrow in scope (2 RL training domains: HotpotQA-variant and Big-Math), and larger-scale/production-relevant reasoning benchmarks (e.g., competition math, code) are not tested, limiting certainty about broader generalization of the method to more diverse and harder reasoning tasks.

strengths: Clean theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 (and its generalization in Appendix A via Savage-Dawid representation) rigorously establishes that a combined correctness + bounded proper scoring rule reward simultaneously incentivizes calibration and correctness, and explains why unbounded scores like log-loss fail this property — a nice, non-trivial piece of decision theory grounding for a practical RL method.

Thorough empirical evaluation across two very different domains (multi-hop QA and math) with multiple out-of-domain generalization datasets (7 total datasets), and a wide set of baselines (BCE classifier, Brier classifier, linear probe, answer-probability), making the comparison reasonably comprehensive.

The finding that RLVR degrades calibration OOD while RLCR improves it, despite comparable in-domain accuracy, is a clear and practically important result with real implications for trustworthy reasoning models.

Interesting and well-motivated downstream analyses: confidence-weighted test-time scaling (best-of-N, majority vote), coherence/self-consistency of confidence across multiple reasoning chains, and probing whether the CoT analysis itself carries calibration-relevant information (Section 4.5) — these extend the paper beyond a single headline metric.

Reasonably transparent about limitations (e.g., SFT+RLCR losing OOD accuracy, residual overconfidence, inter-solution inconsistency), and includes detailed reproducibility information (prompts, training/evaluation setup) in the appendix.
weaknesses: Single base model (Qwen2.5-7B) and single RL algorithm (GRPO variant) are used throughout; no experiments at different scales or with other model families, so it's unclear how well the theoretical guarantees translate into practice as model size/capability changes (the capacity-dependent classifier result in Fig. 5 suggests this could matter significantly).

The RLCR accuracy is sometimes on par with or very slightly below RLVR (e.g., 62.1% vs 63.0% on HotpotQA, 72.7% vs 72.9% on Big-Math) rather than clearly matching it; while differences are small, the paper's framing ('no loss in accuracy') is only loosely supported and lacks statistical significance testing or variance across seeds.

The SFT+RLCR variant shows a fairly large OOD accuracy drop (e.g., 50.9%→43.8% averaged, and dramatic drops on GPQA/CommonsenseQA in Table 7), attributed informally to 'catastrophic forgetting' without deeper investigation — this weakens the practical takeaway of the SFT warmup component, which is otherwise presented as a positive contribution for math calibration.

Reliance on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as an automatic judge for several benchmarks (TriviaQA, SimpleQA, CommonsenseQA, GPQA) introduces potential noise/bias into both accuracy and correctness-conditioned calibration metrics, with no human validation or inter-rater agreement reported.

Absolute out-of-domain calibration remains poor even after RLCR (e.g., ECE around 0.21-0.25 in Table 1), and the swarm plot in Fig. 6b shows persistent overconfidence OOD; the paper is upfront about this but it somewhat undercuts the strength of the calibration improvement narrative.

The novelty relative to closely related RL-with-proper-scoring-rule works (Xu et al. 2024; Stangel et al. 2025) is incremental — the core technical delta is adding a correctness reward term with a boundedness argument, which, while theoretically clean, is a relatively modest extension over existing calibration-RL literature.

Some experimental design choices are only partially justified, e.g., using different system prompts (Long RLCR vs Simple RLCR) for HotpotQA vs Math based on what 'worked better,' which could reflect prompt-sensitivity in ways not fully characterized.
